title: Like cotton in the wind
hookLine: let the mind be led by effort as cotton is lifted by the wind (Bodhicaryavatara 7)
tomorrow: where does Shantideva go when life gets loud?

cards: A dandelion seed on a breezy day doesn't try to fly. It has no muscles and no plan. It has a shape that catches the wind, and the wind does the rest.
Watch one long enough and it seems to choose its way. It doesn't. Some good habits work like that: the evening walk that happens without a debate, the Sunday call to a grandparent.
Near the end of his chapter on effort, Shantideva gives his answer to what keeps you going, and it's just as light.

teach.h: COTTON GOES WHERE THE WIND GOES.
teach.b: His answer is a tuft of cotton. Just as cotton goes wherever the wind carries it, he says, let yourself be carried by enthusiasm, and strength comes. The secret isn't more force.
It's becoming light enough to be lifted. Delight in the good, built up day by day, becomes a wind of its own, and you stop having to decide every time. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In the Hebrew Bible, the book of Ecclesiastes, in the King James English: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might."
Shared ground: both say give the good in front of you your whole self, today, without holding back. One honest difference.
Ecclesiastes gives its reason in the same verse: there is no work in the grave, so do it now, in this one life.
Shantideva's reason is the long road to awakening for all beings, which Buddhists see as walked across many lives, carried more by joy than by the clock. Two reasons, and the same lift.

how: Buddhist teachers often describe practice becoming easier as it turns into habit carried by joy; Shantideva's cotton image closes the practical advice of his effort chapter.

games.q: what does “like cotton in the wind” mean?
o: drifting wherever life happens to take you
effort grown light enough to be carried by joy
giving up control and letting others decide

games.q: the wind and the hand — tap the pairs.
p: this one life, or awakening for all

s: Shantideva says effort works best when you force it harder
his image is cotton lifted by wind: effort grown light, carried by enthusiasm.
Ecclesiastes 9:10 tells its reader to do what the hand finds to do with might
"whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might."
Ecclesiastes and Shantideva give the same reason for wholehearted work
the verse points to this one life before the grave; Shantideva to awakening for all beings.

games.q: a classmate says, 'Ecclesiastes and Shantideva both say work hard, so it's all the same idea.' what's a fair reply?
o: they share 'give the good in front of you your all'; the reasons differ: this life, or awakening.
yes, every tradition teaches exactly the same thing in different words.
no, they share nothing; one speaks of God and the other doesn't.
games.why: shared ground, honestly stated: wholehearted work. and one honest difference: Ecclesiastes' reason is this one life; Shantideva's is awakening for all beings.

practice: Find something light near you: a tissue, a scrap of paper, a loose thread. Rest it on your open palm and breathe out gently across it, and watch it lift with no effort of its own.
Then name one good habit you'd like to carry you that way, small enough to happen without a debate.

wordCard.voice: Like cotton in the wind: Shantideva's picture of effort grown light, carried by enthusiasm instead of pushed by force.

carryVoice: The line: lifted by the wind, light enough to be carried, like a seed on a breeze. Chapter seven, finished.
